To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the decomposition rate of roots from different crops was related to their chemical composition and that the chemical characteristics (traits, i.e., N and hemicellulose contents) were able to predict the root quality and decomposition.

the chemical composition of roots from different plant families, as for the aerial parts of plants, is a key factor in determining their rate of decomposition and that the chemical composition is a key factor to predict the contribution of roots to the C sequestration in soil.
the chemical composition of roots is a good predictor of their rate of decomposition.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of roots in the C cycle and provides a basis for a better assessment of root C contribution to the soil.
the role of roots in the soil C sequestration.
understanding the role of plant traits in the decomposition process, which is an essential component of the carbon cycle in terrestrial ecosystems.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
root C mineralization depends on the chemical composition of roots and on plant family.
roots from Poaceae are more resistant than other roots.
roots of grasses, with their high hemicellulosic content and low N content, are of low quality and decompose slowly.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
root C mineralization is a function of the chemical composition of roots and that the botanical families can help to predict it.
the quality of root biomass is a function of its chemical composition and that this chemical composition is strongly influenced by the botanical family of the crop.
the chemical composition of roots is a key factor to predict the fate of root C in soils.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the C mineralization in soil is strongly influenced by the chemical traits of roots, and that this is not a random process but a highly predictable one, which is a key to the understanding of the C cycle.
roots from grass species have a low quality and a low contribution to soil carbon sequestration.
the C mineralization rate and the amount of C mineralizable in soil are strongly related to root chemical traits and to their botanical affiliation.
